{"title":"Folio Finch awareness content: stock records vs display notes","summary":"Platform-ready awareness content that clarifies the practical difference between a stock record and a display note, using Folio Finch’s fictional postcard example and referencing Shelf Notes as a 35-minute live online demonstration without adding CTAs or extra event details.","sections":[{"id":"linkedin-stock-vs-display-notes","type":"linkedin","title":"LinkedIn post: Stock record vs display note","platform":"LinkedIn","body":"If your stock record is doing the job of a display note, something will always feel slightly off.

A stock record answers: what is held.
A display note answers: how the item is presented.

They are related, but they are not interchangeable.

A stock record is built for accuracy and continuity.
It keeps details stable as items move through receiving, counting, replenishment, and reporting.

A display note is built for the floor.
It captures the decisions that make a display coherent: grouping, signage language, placement, handling notes, and any context that helps the team present the item consistently.

Here is a clean way to separate them using a fictional postcard range as an example:

Stock record (what is held)
- Item name and variant
- Supplier or source
- SKU or internal code
- Unit cost and retail price
- Quantity on hand and reorder triggers

Display note (how it is presented)
- Where it lives on the shop floor
- Which titles it is grouped with
- The short line on the label, if you use one
- Display style notes, for example face-out vs stacked

Folio Finch’s Shelf Notes is a 35-minute live online demonstration led by Mira, comparing a stock record with a display note using that fictional postcard range. It is a demonstration, not an inventory audit or a shop-specific consultation.

A stock record is not a display note.

A stock record is for continuity: what you have, what it costs, what needs replenishing.
A display note is for presentation: how the item shows up on the floor, with what, and where.

Example (fictional): a postcard range.
Stock record tracks the variants and quantities.
Display note captures the grouping and the label line that makes the set feel intentional.

Shelf Notes from Folio Finch is a 35-minute live online demonstration led by Mira that compares the two using a fictional postcard range. It is a demonstration, not an audit or a consultation.

Caption 2
When the team asks, “Where does this belong?”, your stock record is not the best place to answer.

Stock records describe what is held.
Display notes describe how it is presented.

Keeping them separate reduces friction. One stays stable for counting and ordering. The other stays practical for the floor and signage.

Shelf Notes is a 35-minute live online demonstration from Folio Finch, led by Mira, showing the difference with a fictional postcard range.

Caption 3
Two documents. Two jobs.

Stock record = accuracy over time.
Display note = consistency on the floor.

If a display needs a tiny rule, it belongs in a display note. If it needs to be counted, it belongs in the stock record.

Hi,

In museum shops, two useful documents often get blended together, and it creates quiet friction.

A stock record describes what is held.
It is designed for accuracy over time, so it can support receiving, counting, replenishment, and reporting.

A display note describes how an item is presented.
It is designed for consistency on the shop floor, so the team can set up, label, and maintain a display the same way across shifts.

A simple way to keep them separate:

Stock record (what is held)
- Item name and variant
- Supplier or source
- SKU or internal code
- Unit cost and retail price
- Quantity on hand

Display note (how it is presented)
- Floor location
- Grouping rules
- Label line, if you use one
- Presentation notes, for example face-out vs stacked

Folio Finch’s Shelf Notes is a 35-minute live online demonstration led by Mira, comparing a stock record with a display note using a fictional postcard range as the example. It is a demonstration, not an inventory audit or a shop-specific consultation.

Keeping each document in its lane keeps the record clean and the display easier to run.
